title: Regret-aware kernel catalog pruner with chiplet-aware fallback
creator: Evelyn Chen
description:
Problem: Our kernel recommendation engine currently exposes a large candidate set for each (arch, model, seqlen) bucket which increases decision latency and makes online exploration noisy. When we aggressively explore new microkernels (especially on emerging chiplet/SLICE topologies), transient regressions cause customer-facing latency spikes.

Proposal: Implement a lightweight 'catalog pruner' that maintains a compact candidate list per fingerprint (architecture + seqlen + model family) by removing kernels with persistent regret while retaining a safety fence of conservative fallbacks. The pruner operates in two modes: offline consolidation (batch analysis of historical telemetry) and online graceful decay (age-based eviction controlled by regret statistics). The system is chiplet-aware: for chiplet/partitioned devices we prefer kernels that avoid cross-tile synchronization unless a clear expected-latency improvement outweighs the added risk.

Key ideas and heuristics:
- Regret signal: compute a running regret score per kernel from the observed latency-cost tradeoff versus the current incumbent. Use an exponentially weighted moving average of latency + normalized token-cost with a heavier weight on p95 latency for customer safety.
- Eviction threshold: remove a kernel from the active candidate list when regret exceeds a tunable threshold for N consecutive assessment windows or when sample count > M and confidence interval excludes being top-k.
- Safety fence: always keep at least 2 conservative kernels per bucket (incumbent + stable fallback). Conservative kernels are selected by historical stability score rather than raw latency.
- Chiplet-aware penalty: apply a multiplicative penalty to expected improvement when the kernel requires inter-chiplet memory transfers or synchronization. This prevents us from favoring kernels that look fast on microbenchmarks but regress under real cross-tile workloads.
- Warmstart and reincarnation: evicted kernels are archived with metadata and can be reintroduced via a warmed trial if new telemetry suggests a shift (model update, quantization change, driver update).
- Exploration policy: use a low-rate contextual bandit (epsilon-decay with time-dependent schedule and a regret-prioritized replay buffer) to occasionally surface archived kernels for short probe windows with rollback on safety signals.

Telemetry and metrics:
- Inputs: per-request kernel id, arch fingerprint, seqlen, model id, latency (p50/p95/p99), token_cost, error/oom flags, GPU topology tags (chiplet/partitioning), trace id for correlation.
- Outputs: candidate list size per bucket, eviction events, regret_histogram, rollback_count, customer-impact incidents attributed to pruner decisions.
- SLOs to monitor: p95 latency drift (<= +5% vs baseline), rollback rate (< 1% of trials), RPC error/oom increase (none tolerated), cost per token trend (expected decrease for successful prunes).

Rollout plan:
1) Offline simulation: run pruner logic over last 90 days of telemetry in staging to measure false-positive evictions and compare simulated p95 with live baseline.
2) Canary: enable pruner for 1% of low-risk traffic on a single region and monitor rollback_count and latency distribution for two weeks.
3) Gradual ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 20% with automated revert on guardrail violations.
4) Full enablement for new buckets only (legacy buckets opt-in) to limit blast radius.

Testing strategy:
- Synthetic workloads: replay customer-seqlen traces with injected chiplet-contention to validate chiplet penalty behavior.
- Long-tail soak: 72h soak on mixed workloads capturing bursts and model-version transitions.
- A/B experiments: compare candidate-set sizes vs control and measure cost/latency tradeoffs.

Open design decisions and trade-offs:
- Regret formula weighting: currently we plan p95*0.7 + normalized_cost*0.3; we need product input whether cost savings should have higher weight for non-SaaS internal customers.
- Eviction conservativeness: default window N=3 is chosen to reduce noisy evictions but slows adaptation; product feedback required.
- Archive lifespan: how long to keep evicted kernels before GC? Proposal: 90 days with extended retention for kernels evicted due to driver bugs (manual tag).

Operational runbook summary:
- On rollback or p95 spike: immediately disable pruner for the affected bucket and surface an incident to SRE with link to the candidate list snapshot.
- If chiplet-flagged regressions appear: temporarily raise chiplet penalty coefficient and run a warmstart trial for conservative kernels.

Deliverables and milestones:
- Design doc (this ticket), offline simulator, pruner service + controlplane API, canary instrumentation dashboards, automated rollback hook, and postmortem template.

References and artifacts:
- Confluence design: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Regret+Pruner+Design
- Offline simulator PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1427
- Canary dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/Pruner/canary-traffic

Expected outcome: Reduce active candidate list sizes by ~40% for stable buckets, cut decision overhead for kernel selection, and lower unit-cost by enabling faster convergence to stable low-cost kernels while preserving latency SLOs via conservative safety fences.
